concept.name: Monte Carlo simulation
concept.definition: The use of repeated random sampling to approximate quantities that are difficult to compute analytically, such as expectations, distributions of estimators, option prices, or the sampling variability of a trading rule, by generating many pseudo-random realizations and averaging. Named and systematized by Metropolis and Ulam (1949).
concept.intuition: If you cannot solve the probability problem on paper, play it out thousands of times with a random number generator and use the empirical frequencies as the answer.
concept.mechanics: Draw pseudo-random samples from the assumed model, compute the quantity of interest on each draw, and average; the Monte Carlo error falls as 1/sqrt(N), so accuracy is controlled by the replication count. Variance-reduction techniques (antithetic variates, control variates, importance sampling) improve efficiency.
concept.formula: E[g(X)] approximately (1/N) sum_{i=1}^N g(X_i) with X_i drawn from the target distribution; the standard error of the estimate is sd(g(X))/sqrt(N).
concept.failure_modes: Answers are only as good as the model being simulated: Monte Carlo propagates rather than fixes wrong distributional assumptions, such as Gaussian draws understating tail risk. Rare-event estimates converge slowly without importance sampling.
concept.misconceptions: That a more sophisticated generator removes model risk: simulation explores the implications of assumed dynamics but does not validate them against reality.
concept.example: Estimating a path-dependent option price: simulate 100,000 price paths under the model, compute the discounted payoff on each, and average, with a standard error read from the spread of payoffs.
